nameStory: The Black-tailed Gull gets its name from the distinctive broad black band across its white tail - a feature that makes it stand out among the gull family. This marking is so prominent that early naturalists who first described the species chose it as the defining characteristic for the bird's common name.
description: The Black-tailed Gull is a medium-sized seabird native to the coastlines of East Asia that occasionally shows up as a rare visitor to New England shores. It's roughly the size of a Ring-billed Gull, with clean white plumage, gray wings, and that telltale black tail band. With only 10 recorded sightings in New England, spotting one here is like finding a feathered treasure from across the Pacific Ocean.

idTips.label: Black tail band
idTips.description: Look for a crisp black band across the white tail that's visible both when perched and in flight - no other gull in our region has this striking pattern

idTips.label: Yellow-tipped bill
idTips.description: The thick yellow bill has a bright red spot near the tip and often shows a black ring, giving it a colorful, almost painted appearance

idTips.label: Bright yellow legs
idTips.description: The legs are a vivid yellow-orange color that looks almost like it's been dipped in bright paint - much more intense than most gulls

idTips.label: Dark eye with red rim
idTips.description: The dark eye is surrounded by a thin red orbital ring that gives the bird an alert, almost stern expression

idTips.label: Compact build
idTips.description: Smaller and more compact than a Herring Gull, with proportionally shorter wings and a rounder head shape

habitat: In New England, Black-tailed Gulls are most likely spotted along rocky coastlines, harbors, and beaches where they might mix with flocks of more common gulls. They prefer areas with jetties, piers, and fishing activity where they can scavenge for food. Look for them at major birding hotspots along the coast, particularly during migration periods.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare visitor during spring migration, most likely to appear at coastal locations in late April through May when vagrant seabirds sometimes show up.
seasonality.summer: Summer sightings are possible but exceptionally rare, usually involving individual birds that have wandered far from their normal Pacific range.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration offers the best chance for sightings, particularly September through November when storm systems can blow off-course migrants toward our shores.
seasonality.winter: Winter records exist but are very uncommon; any winter gull flocks should be carefully checked as vagrants sometimes linger for extended periods.

funFact: Black-tailed Gulls can live over 20 years and show remarkable site fidelity, returning to the exact same nesting colonies in Japan and Korea year after year - so the individual birds spotted in New England are true oceanic adventurers that have traveled roughly 6,000 miles from home!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Ring-billed or Herring Gulls at a distance, but that distinctive black tail band is a dead giveaway - no other gull species in North America has this feature. Remember: "Black tail, rare tale" - if you see that black band, you're looking at something very special.
contextualKnowledge: Black-tailed Gulls are considered "mega-rarities" in North America, meaning any sighting should be carefully documented with photos and reported to birding authorities. What you're seeing represents one of the most significant birding finds possible in New England - these birds have somehow crossed the entire Pacific Ocean to reach our shores.
compareHints: Unlike Ring-billed Gulls which have a black ring on a yellow bill, Black-tailed Gulls have a red spot and often a black band near the bill tip. Compared to Herring Gulls, they're smaller with much brighter yellow legs and that diagnostic black tail band. The combination of compact size, vivid yellow legs, and especially that black tail stripe separates them from all other large white-headed gulls in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's large gulls, American Herring Gulls are the 'Goldilocks' species - not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls, not as small as Ring-billed Gulls, but just right in the middle.
Ring-billed Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, lacking the Herring Gull's robust build and pink legs.

Among New England gulls, Great Black-backed Gulls dwarf the common Herring Gull in size and have much darker backs, while Ring-billed Gulls are significantly smaller with lighter grey backs and distinctive black rings around their bills.
Among New England's large gulls, Iceland Gulls are unique for their combination of medium size and extremely pale wing tips.
Among the large white-headed gulls, Lesser Black-backed Gulls are distinguished by their uniquely dark backs - darker than Herring Gulls but not as massive as Great Black-backed Gulls.
Among New England's large gulls, Glaucous Gulls stand out for their pale wingtips—Herring Gulls and Great Black-backed Gulls both have bold black wingtips, while Ring-billed Gulls are much smaller.
Common Gulls are smaller and more delicate than Herring Gulls, with yellow-green (not orange-red) bills and legs, plus a gentler facial expression.
Compared to the common Herring Gull, the Slaty-backed Gull has a noticeably darker slate-gray back and is generally larger and more robust.
Compared to the common Ring-billed Gull, Short-billed Gulls are smaller with cleaner wing tips and lack any dark markings on the bill.
Among the large white-headed gulls in its genus, the California Gull is most similar to the Ring-billed and Herring Gulls but sits between them in size.
Unlike the common white-bodied gulls of New England like Herring and Ring-billed Gulls, Heermann's Gull has the reverse color scheme with a dark body and white head.
